title: Odds-Shift Slippage in One-vs-Rest Rankers: Diagnosing and Repairing Reweighting-Induced Top-𝐾 Errors

paper.title: Odds-Shift Slippage in One-vs-Rest Rankers: Diagnosing and Repairing Reweighting-Induced Top- K K Errors
paper.abstract: Abstract. One-vs-rest rankers that show each user the top- K K of many rare labels usually counter imbalance with a per-label positive-class weight, scale_pos_weight = n − / n + =n_{-}/n_{+} . Elkan’s identity says such a weight shifts label j j ’s log-odds by ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} , so the model ranks by weighted odds rather than by the marginal that is Bayes-optimal for precision@ K K , and it suggests inverting the shift afterwards; what a finite learner does with a weight in the thousands, and which repair then works, has not been measured. We call the gap between the promised shift and the realized one odds-shift slippage and measure it on matched pairs of LightGBM and MLP models that differ only in the weights. On Santander the weight takes MAP ​ @ ​ 7 \mathrm{MAP}@7 from 0.808 0.808 to 0.117 0.117 ; for the boosted pairs the ideal odds shift accounts for 23% of that loss (32% on Instacart; 98% for an MLP pair on the same rows) and slippage for the rest. We prove that a booster whose leaf steps are capped at c c realizes at most T ​ η ​ c T\eta c nat of shift in T T rounds at rate η \eta , which a cap sweep confirms, and show that without a cap saturated cells tie at exactly 1.0 1.0 , beyond the reach of any separable map. The analytic inversion therefore pays only where the shift was realized and nothing saturated, whereas per-label isotonic regression returns the Santander model to 0.784 0.784 ( 0.780 0.780 with the calibrator fitted on the validation period) — but only if labels without calibration positives are mapped to their prior rather than passed through. On 11 public MULAN benchmarks and 5 learners the weighted model loses more than half of its MAP ​ @ ​ K \mathrm{MAP}@K in 8 of 55 cells, and on delicious and Corel5k the same repair returns it to the unweighted level; per-label calibration hurts where positives are scarce, a harm that a cross-validated rule removes for the default learner. The recipe — estimate marginals unweighted, calibrate per label with an explicit prior fallback, choose the calibrator on the calibration split, then decide at top- K K — is released as oddslip .

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text: Ranking many binary labels within a row is the operational core of product recommendation, tagging and risk triage: for each customer the system scores every product, sorts, and shows the top K K ( Jain et al., 2016 ; Menon et al., 2019 ) . The labels are almost always imbalanced, and the most common remedy in gradient-boosting practice is a per-label positive-class weight, scale_pos_weight in XGBoost and LightGBM ( Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ; Ke et al., 2017 ) , for which the XGBoost documentation suggests n − / n + n_{-}/n_{+} ( XGBoost developers, 2026 ) ; neural multi-label models use the same recipe as pos_weight . Label-specific weights are not a free choice when the deliverable is a per-row ranking. Ranking labels by their marginal p i ​ j = Pr ⁡ ( y i ​ j = 1 ∣ x i ) p_{ij}=\Pr(y_{ij}=1\mid x_{i}) is Bayes-optimal for precision@ K K , and one-vs-rest training with a proper loss is consistent for it ( Menon et al., 2019 ; Wydmuch et al., 2018 ) . A positive-class weight w w moves the population minimizer of a proper loss from p p to w ​ p / ( w ​ p + 1 − p ) wp/(wp+1-p) , an odds shift by w w ( Elkan, 2001 ; Saerens et al., 2002 ) . Together the two facts say that a label-specific w j w_{j} makes the model rank by w j ⋅ odds ⁡ ( p i ​ j ) w_{j}\cdot\mathrm{odds}(p_{ij}) , a different ranking whenever the weights differ. What the classical account leaves open is what a finite learner does when w j w_{j} is in the thousands, as the recommended value is for rare labels, and which post-hoc repair then works. Independent per-class calibration maps are known to lose top- k k accuracy in multi-class settings ( Patel et al., 2021 ) , and the extreme multi-label literature deliberately uses one shared monotone map, deferring per-label calibration to future work ( Ullah et al., 2025 ) . Neither measures the cross-label consequence of training weights on a top- K K benchmark, nor what a calibrator does with labels that have no calibration positives. Figure 2 gives our answer on two product-recommendation benchmarks, Santander and Instacart, each on a pair of LightGBM models that differ only in the weights. Applying the ideal odds shift to the unweighted model reproduces only a minority of the loss the trained weighted model actually suffers. We call the remainder odds-shift slippage : the shift the learner realizes is not the shift the weight asked for. Figure 1 sketches the two regimes that produce it. A leaf-step cap keeps the realized shift below ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} ( Proposition 2.4 ); without a cap the learner realizes the shift on the labels where it is still defined, while elsewhere cells saturate into ties that no per-label map can reorder ( Lemma 2.3 ). Among the configurations we evaluated, analytic inversion improves only those that combine a near-intended realized shift with no observed saturation ( Figure 3 ); per-label calibration repairs the ordered part, provided that a label without calibration positives is mapped to its prior rather than passed through ( Remark 2 ).

sections.heading: Contributions
sections.text: (1) Odds-shift slippage, decomposed. Using Elkan’s identity as a what-if device, we split the top- K K loss of a weighted one-vs-rest ranker into the ideal odds shift and the loss beyond it, the slippage, which itself splits into the component that a per-label monotone map fitted on calibration data recovers and a residue above the in-sample per-label ceiling ( Figure 2 A, Table 1 ). For the boosted pairs the shift accounts for 23% of the observed loss on Santander ( 20.3 ± 2.3 % 20.3\pm 2.3\% over three train-row draws) and 32% on Instacart; the share is a property of the pair, since an MLP pair on the same Santander rows gives up 98% of its loss to the same ideal shift. Logit adjustment and residual reranking ( Menon et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) correct a trained score; neither measures how far a training weight’s intended shift was realized, which is what the decomposition isolates. (2) A step budget that makes the account falsifiable. Proposition 2.4 bounds the realized per-label shift of a booster with leaf-step cap c c by T ​ η ​ c T\eta c whatever the weight, and Corollary 2.5 says when the analytic inversion is exact. A sweep of 5 caps on both benchmarks keeps every realized maximum inside its budget with no saturation ( Figure 2 B); without a cap the shift is identifiable only on labels with no saturated cell, where its median is close to ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} . Among the evaluated models the inversion pays only for the two that realized most of the shift and saturated nothing ( Figure 3 ), an association rather than a proven condition; and an unweighted twin trained with the same cap matches the calibrated capped weighted arm, so on Santander, the one dataset with such twins, the cap, not the weight, is what helps; we know of no earlier statement of when the analytic inversion ( Elkan, 2001 ) can be exact for a booster under a leaf-step cap. (3) Per-label calibration with a prior fallback is the repair that travels, with its selection rule. Per-label isotonic regression with dead labels mapped to their prior returns the weighted Santander booster to within 0.003 0.003 of its in-sample ceiling under the test-split protocol and within 0.01 0.01 under the deployment protocol; a shared map repairs nothing beyond tie resolution ( Remark 1 ), and the identity fallback turns the same calibrator into a loss ( Remark 2 ). The collapse and its repair reproduce on 11 MULAN benchmarks and 5 learners ( Figure 4 ), where the calibrator also hurts an unweighted model with scarce calibration positives; a cross-validated choice inside the calibration split removes that harm for the default learner and fails in 6 of 110 cells. Per-label monotone maps are known ( Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002 ; Tae and Lee, 2026 ) ; what is new is the source of the distortion, the fallback that decides the sign, and the selection by the deployed metric.

sections.heading: Data and models.
sections.text: The Santander Product Recommendation data ( Kaggle and Banco Santander, 2016 ) has 24 products. We sort the public training file by date and cut it at fixed row-count fractions into 8,248,933 training, 1,903,599 validation (held out from fitting, preceding the test period) and 2,538,132 test rows; the label of a row is the set of products added in the following month, and MAP ​ @ ​ 7 \mathrm{MAP}@7 follows the Kaggle definition on the rows with at least one added product (2.9% of the 1,776,693 evaluation rows). LGBM-w and LGBM-0 are LightGBM one-vs-rest models trained by one script with identical configuration (60 trees, learning rate 0.05 0.05 , 31 leaves, no subsampling, one seed, the same features and split); the only difference is that LGBM-w sets w j = n − , j / n + , j w_{j}=n_{-,j}/n_{+,j} per label (between 78 and 8,248,932) and LGBM-0 sets no weight. WGB (Wasserstein gradient boosting ( Matsubara, 2024 ) ) estimates probabilities directly without weights (Supplement Table S1). The test-split (diagnostic) protocol fits calibrators on a random 30% of the test rows (seed 42, 761,439 rows) and evaluates on the remaining 70%; it is optimistic for deployment, and its gain on the unweighted model ( + 0.012 ​ [ + 0.011 , + 0.013 ] +0.012~[+0.011,\,+0.013] ) bounds what the protocol itself contributes. Supplement Table S5 sweeps the split size. The deployment protocol fits calibrators on the validation period and evaluates on all test rows (Supplement Table S3). Under the test-split protocol 3 labels have no calibration positives and every calibrated label has at least 1 (median 136). Bootstrap intervals use B = 2000 B=2000 per-row resamples of the 51,403 evaluation rows with a positive. One instrument matters for every saturation number below: predictions are stored as single-precision probabilities, so a cell “at exactly 1.0 1.0 ” is one whose raw margin reaches 17.3 17.3 nat, the float32 rounding threshold below one. Every saturation share is a property of that stored array, the object a deployed ranker consumes; a pipeline that keeps the raw margin can still order those cells, a calibrator of the probabilities cannot. The Instacart 2017 data ( Instacart, 2017 ) has 49,688 products and, for 131,209 users, an ordered history of prior orders. We use it as a next-order ranking task in the form of the next-basket literature ( Section 5 ): one row per user and reference order, features from the orders before it only (8,320 columns), a within-user chronological split (third-last order for training, second-last as validation period, last as test period; 131,209 rows each), and the set of products in the reference order as the label. The label set is the top-4,000 products by training frequency, the budget of one LightGBM fit per label and configuration; the Kaggle task is not comparable. The weights range from 6 to 2,301 ( ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} from 1.8 to 7.7); the calibration split has 39,362 rows, 0 dead labels and a median of 37 positives per label, and popularity ranking scores 0.056 0.056 . The LightGBM pair uses the Santander configuration; both boosters start from the same initial score logit ⁡ π ^ j \operatorname{logit}\hat{\pi}_{j} , as Proposition 2.4 assumes. The second learner is a shared-trunk MLP (two hidden layers of width 256, binary cross-entropy with per-label pos_weight ∈ { 1 , r j } \in\{1,r_{j}\} , 20 epochs, no early stopping, seed 42) on the same rows and labels; on Instacart it scores all 49,688 products in one model, of which the top-4,000 columns enter Table 1 (all-product ladder: Supplement S7).

sections.heading: Decomposition and repair ladder ( Figure 2 A, Table 1 ).
sections.text: For this pair the weighted model loses 0.690 0.690 MAP ​ @ ​ 7 \mathrm{MAP}@7 against LGBM-0 ; we express every repair as the share of this loss it returns. Adding ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} to the logits of LGBM-0 is the ideal weighted model of Proposition 2.1 ; it scores 0.646 0.646 , keeps 3.11 of 7 items of the unweighted top-7, and accounts for 23% of the observed loss. The trained LGBM-w keeps only 2.57 of 7 items, has 16.6% of its cells at exactly 1.0 1.0 , and the analytic inversion with the known w j w_{j} returns 5% ( 0.151 0.151 ). The ladder measures how much of the remaining distortion a per-label monotone map recovers, rung by rung. An intercept-only logit shift fitted per label on the calibration split returns 90% ( 0.738 0.738 ), so for most labels the realized distortion is close to a constant — but not the constant ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} . Supplement Fig. S1 shows why label by label: the prevalence-matching shift b j b_{j} equals ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} on the labels whose cells never saturate (median b j / ln ⁡ w j = 0.98 b_{j}/\ln w_{j}=0.98 over 5 of 24 labels), as Proposition 2.1 says, and is not identified on the other 19, whose cells at exactly 1.0 1.0 no finite shift moves (Supplement S7). Per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback returns 97% ( 0.784 0.784 ), within 0.003 0.003 of the in-sample per-label ceiling ( 0.786 0.786 ). The last 3% ( 0.021 0.021 ) lies above that ceiling and is consistent with the saturated cells: re-ordering only the cells at exactly 1.0 1.0 by the unweighted model’s order returns 5% of the loss, an oracle order that reads the test labels 8% (Supplement S7). Three controls guard the comparison. Per-row bootstrap intervals put the gap between LGBM-0 raw and the repaired LGBM-w at + 0.024 ​ [ + 0.022 , + 0.026 ] +0.024~[+0.022,\,+0.026] , and under the same calibrator LGBM-0 itself reaches 0.819 0.819 , so the like-for-like gap is 0.819 − 0.784 0.819-0.784 . The within-label AUC, which no monotone map changes, is 0.824 0.824 for LGBM-0 against 0.793 0.793 for LGBM-w . Pooled isotonic leaves WGB and LGBM-0 unchanged ( Remark 1 ) and moves LGBM-w to 0.261 0.261 only by merging tied cells, which the stable sort then breaks by label index. Trained r \sqrt{r} and 10 ​ r 10r arms behave the same way (raw 0.688 0.688 and 0.036 0.036 , repaired 0.806 0.806 and 0.772 0.772 ).

sections.heading: Instacart: the same decomposition, a larger role for the calibrator.
sections.text: The Instacart pair loses 0.129 0.129 ( 0.131 0.131 to 0.001 0.001 ), keeping 0.02 of 7 items of the unweighted top-7. The ideal odds shift accounts for 32% of that loss and already changes the top-7 of 79% of rows; the rest is slippage. One thing differs: the same calibrator also lifts the unweighted model, from 0.131 0.131 to 0.250 0.250 , because after 60 rounds at learning rate 0.05 0.05 the scores of 4,000 labels are not yet comparable across labels and the per-label maps supply that comparability. The cost of the weight is therefore the like-for-like gap after calibration, 0.250 0.250 against 0.225 0.225 (ceilings 0.269 0.269 against 0.230 0.230 ), not the raw loss. Bootstrap intervals separate every comparison drawn here (repaired weighted model minus its inversion: + 0.208 ​ [ + 0.206 , + 0.210 ] +0.208~[+0.206,\,+0.210] ). sections.heading: Mechanism: cap sweep and inversion regime ( Figure 2 B, Figure 3 ).
sections.text: Re-training the weighted configuration with max_delta_step = c ∈ { 0.3 , 0.7 , 1 , 2 , 5 } =c\in\{0.3,0.7,1,2,5\} ( T = 60 T=60 , η = 0.05 \eta=0.05 ) bounds the realized shift by T ​ η ​ c T\eta c , from 0.9 0.9 to 15.0 15.0 nat, against ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} up to 15.9 15.9 on Santander and 7.7 7.7 on Instacart. Proposition 2.4 survives every cell of the sweep: the largest realized shift stays inside the budget at all 5 caps on both datasets, tightly at the smallest cap ( 0.90 0.90 against 0.9 0.9 on Santander) and with room to spare at the largest ( 8.90 8.90 against 15.0 15.0 ), and no cell sits at exactly 1.0 1.0 under any cap. The budget’s falsifiable content is the over-correction it forces on the inversion, whose median ln ⁡ w j − b j \ln w_{j}-b_{j} falls from 7.0 7.0 nat at c = 0.3 c=0.3 to 1.1 1.1 nat at c = 5 c=5 on Santander (Supplement S7). Figure 3 says when the analytic inversion works: the inversion pays only for the two models that realized the shift and saturated nothing (Santander c = 5 c=5 , raw 0.718 0.718 to 0.806 0.806 against 0.808 0.808 for LGBM-0 ; the Instacart MLP below), it over-corrects where the cap starved the shift and barely moves the uncapped models, whose ties no separable map reaches. The repair does not travel down the sweep unchanged either: per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback is the best rung at all 5 Instacart caps and at 3 of 5 Santander caps, but at c = 0.3 c=0.3 it is the worst rung of that model ( 0.556 0.556 against 0.634 0.634 for doing nothing), because the cap compresses the scores until the per-label map’s own in-sample reference ( 0.555 0.555 ) sits below raw — the scarcity that the selection rule of Section 6 exists to catch. At c = 5 c=5 the capped, calibrated weighted arm scores 0.829 0.829 , above the uncapped unweighted model under the same calibrator ( 0.819 0.819 ), but an unweighted model trained with the same cap scores 0.823 0.823 raw and 0.829 0.829 calibrated, level with it, and at the other 4 caps the unweighted twin is ahead, by up to + 0.198 +0.198 at c = 0.3 c=0.3 (Supplement S7): the gain is the cap’s, not the weight’s.

sections.heading: Two learners.
sections.text: Where it is identified at all, the realized shift of the two learners agrees: the booster’s median b j / ln ⁡ w j b_{j}/\ln w_{j} is 0.98 0.98 on Santander (5 labels) and 0.88 0.88 on Instacart (394), the Instacart MLP’s is 1.06 1.06 (3644), and a clipping-free estimator (Supplement S7) gives 0.78 0.78 and 0.50 0.50 for the two boosters on a larger label set, so an uncapped learner’s median lies between half of the intended shift and 1.06 1.06 times it. What differs between the pairs is how much of the label set retains a shift (1 of 24 labels on the Santander MLP against 3644 of 4,000 for the Instacart MLP). The same ideal shift costs the two Santander pairs very differently ( 0.766 → 0.127 0.766\to 0.127 for the MLP against 0.808 → 0.646 0.808\to 0.646 for LightGBM, 98% of the loss against 23%): the share measures how large ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} is against the unweighted model’s within-row logit gaps. Downstream everything repeats (23.3% of cells at exactly 1.0 1.0 , the inversion returns 21%, the bold rung ( 0.549 0.549 ) lands on its ceiling ( 0.548 0.548 ), 33% of the loss below the unweighted MLP’s raw score). This is the one pair that meets both conditions of Figure 3 — realized shift at the intended level, saturation negligible — and the inversion accordingly works, taking it from 0.008 0.008 to 0.070 0.070 , past the unweighted twin (the all-product MLP meets the same conditions and inverts too, Supplement S7); per-label isotonic regression does better still ( 0.081 0.081 ). sections.heading: The fallback decides the sign.
sections.text: With the identity fallback, per-label isotonic regression yields 0.465 0.465 on LGBM-w (below the popularity baseline 0.535 0.535 ) and lowers WGB from 0.776 0.776 to 0.434 0.434 : the 3 dead labels keep their raw scores (mean 0.120 0.120 on WGB ) while every calibrated label shrinks to its prevalence (largest mean 0.0106 0.0106 ), so all three sit in the top 7 of 100% of rows, the takeover of Remark 2 . Since scarce calibration positives hurt even with the prior fallback ( Section 4 ), the two effects must be kept apart. With the prior fallback the same calibrator gives 0.784 0.784 on LGBM-w , 0.828 0.828 on WGB ( + 0.052 ​ [ + 0.050 , + 0.054 ] +0.052~[+0.050,\,+0.054] ) and 0.819 0.819 on LGBM-0 ( + 0.012 ​ [ + 0.011 , + 0.013 ] +0.012~[+0.011,\,+0.013] ), each within 0.01 0.01 of its ceiling; exclusion behaves like the prior. sections.heading: MULAN benchmarks ( Figure 4 , Table 2 ).
sections.text: We retrain one-vs-rest models on 11 MULAN datasets ( Tsoumakas et al., 2011 ) (every standard-split dataset in the distribution except the two largest, tmc2007 and Corel16k) with w j ∈ { 1 , r j , r j , 10 ​ r j } w_{j}\in\{1,\sqrt{r_{j}},r_{j},10r_{j}\} and 5 learners: LightGBM in a default and a strongly regularized configuration, XGBoost, ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -regularized logistic regression with sample weights, and a two-layer MLP with per-label pos_weight . The largest weight the sweep reaches is 3149 3149 at w = r w{=}r , three orders of magnitude below Santander’s; it is a dose-response over imbalance magnitude that also covers the label counts of Section 3 . Four regularities hold. (i) The collapse reproduces on public data. At w = r w{=}r the raw score falls below half its unweighted value in 8 of 55 learner cells, on corel5k, delicious, genbase alone. With the default LightGBM delicious goes from 0.419 0.419 to 0.001 0.001 and Corel5k from 0.236 0.236 to 0.000 0.000 , both below their popularity baselines — the shape of Table 1 on a public benchmark. The loss is between labels rather than within them (within-label AUC moves only from 0.752 0.752 to 0.705 0.705 on delicious), and the repair follows the same pattern: per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback reaches 0.434 0.434 and 0.244 0.244 , at or above what the unweighted model attains under the same calibrator, while a shared map reaches only 0.025 0.025 and 0.125 0.125 and the inversion only 0.003 0.003 and 0.001 0.001 . Over all 10 learner cells of delicious and Corel5k the repaired weighted model is within 0.028 0.028 of its unweighted arm and the shared map is never within 0.053 0.053 of it. Corel5k also carries the dead-label half: 39 of its 374 labels have no calibration positives, and the identity fallback gives 0.060 0.060 against the prior’s 0.244 0.244 on the default LightGBM — Remark 2 on a public benchmark, though the gap runs down to 0.000 0.000 on other learners. We have no threshold to offer: enron has the weight spread ( max ⁡ r = 786 \max r=786 ) and bibtex the label count ( L = 159 L=159 ) without collapsing. (ii) Elsewhere the sign is learner-dependent. On the 4 datasets with max ⁡ r < 100 \max r<100 the default LightGBM change at w = r w{=}r is a fall of between − 0.001 -0.001 and − 0.041 -0.041 , while across the 5 learners the sign varies and the spread widens to − 0.146 -0.146 and + 0.010 +0.010 . The default-learner reading is in line with the report that class weighting leaves calibration nearly intact at imbalance ratios below 70 ( Liu, 2026 ) . (iii) The what-if prediction is close where nothing saturates. It is within 0.03 0.03 of the trained weighted model on 8 of 11 datasets; it under-predicts the loss where the trained model saturates (genbase: 0.927 0.927 predicted, 0.868 0.868 trained) and over-predicts it where regularization shrinks the realized shift (enron, strongly regularized), where the inversion then recovers the unweighted ranking ( 0.656 0.656 against 0.653 0.653 at w = 1 w{=}1 ) — the small-data counterpart of Figure 3 . (iv) Ties can arrive without saturation. On medical, strongly regularized, the distinct scores per label fall from 24 24 to 2.7 2.7 between w = 1 w{=}1 and 10 ​ r 10r with 0.00 0.00 % of cells saturated: on data this small the ties that defeat a separable map come from coarse leaves. Leaf-saturation checks and a synthetic study with known marginals (Supplement Tables S8–S10) agree: a realizable learner inverts exactly, LightGBM fails where its cells saturate.

sections.heading: The negative result and the selection rule.
sections.text: With few calibration positives, per-label isotonic regression with the prior fallback hurts an unweighted model. With the default LightGBM at w = 1 w{=}1 it lowers MAP ​ @ ​ K \mathrm{MAP}@K by more than 0.005 0.005 on 3 of 11 datasets, and on 2 of them the paired bootstrap interval excludes zero (birds 0.593 → 0.549 0.593\to 0.549 with a median of 5 calibration positives per label; medical 0.683 → 0.651 0.683\to 0.651 with 1); the median number of calibration positives does not separate the cases (genbase and enron gain with 5 and 6), so no fixed threshold can be recommended. The recipe’s answer is a rule fixed on the calibration split alone: 5-fold cross-validation chooses among per-label isotonic regression with positives threshold τ ∈ { 0 , 1 , 2 , 5 , 10 } \tau\in\{0,1,2,5,10\} (labels with at most τ \tau calibration positives keep the prior), the shared map, and no calibration (Supplement Table S6). For the default LightGBM at w = 1 w{=}1 the rule keeps the raw scores on birds, medical and flags, keeps the per-label gains on genbase and enron, loses to raw with an interval excluding zero on 0 of 11 datasets, and gains with one on delicious ( + 0.016 ​ [ + 0.012 , + 0.020 ] +0.016~[+0.012,\,+0.020] ). It is not infallible: across all 110 cells the selection ends more than 0.01 0.01 below raw in 6 (against 29 for the fixed τ = 0 \tau=0 rule); in its worst cell ( − 0.134 -0.134 ) raw and the selected candidate are indistinguishable out of fold yet differ on the test file (Supplement S2).

sections.heading: The odds shift, and what a learner does with it.
sections.text: Elkan’s identity ( Elkan, 2001 ) and the prior-shift correction of ( Saerens et al., 2002 ) describe a positive-class weight as a shift of the log-odds by ln ⁡ w \ln w ; logit adjustment applies that shift post hoc in long-tailed classification ( Menon et al., 2021 ) , label-shift adaptation estimates the shift from a black-box predictor ( Lipton et al., 2018 ) or combines it with calibration ( Alexandari et al., 2020 ) , of which our prevalence-matching shift is the per-label special case, and the inversion the identity suggests is the first repair a practitioner reaches for; Caplin et al. ( Caplin et al., 2022 ) already observe that it fails on a trained binary classifier and recover probabilities through a model of the learner, whereas we measure the realized shift directly and bound it under a cap. The identity describes the population minimizer. Importance weights lose their effect on learners that can fit the weighted objective ( Byrd and Lipton, 2019 ) ; cost-sensitive boosting recovers the posterior ratio only near the decision boundary ( Masnadi-Shirazi and Vasconcelos, 2011 ) , is matched by calibrating an unweighted booster and thresholding ( Nikolaou et al., 2016 ) , and depends on the model being well specified ( Dmochowski et al., 2010 ) , all for one binary decision rather than a ranking across labels; probability estimates are unreliable under imbalance ( Wallace and Dahabreh, 2012 ) and under its corrections ( van den Goorbergh et al., 2022 ) ; a binary tree-ensemble study at imbalance ratios up to 70 finds, in a class-weight control, that class weighting, unlike resampling, barely moves calibration ( Liu, 2026 ) ; it measures calibration rather than a cross-label ranking, and our default-learner results at max ⁡ r < 100 \max r<100 are consistent with it while other learners are not. Long-tailed recognition adjusts the classifier after unweighted training ( Kang et al., 2020 ; Menon et al., 2021 ) within one softmax; we rank labels across independent one-vs-rest models, where the per-label weight is the distortion. Elkan already notes that rebalancing barely changes a decision tree, an early qualitative form of slippage; none of these measures how far a gradient booster ( Friedman, 2001 ) realizes the shift when w j w_{j} is in the thousands.

sections.heading: Consistency and top- K K .
sections.text: One-vs-rest surrogates are consistent for the rank loss ( Dembczyński et al., 2012 ) and, with a proper loss, for precision@ k k ( Menon et al., 2019 ; Wydmuch et al., 2018 ) ; propensity-scored metrics weight labels deliberately ( Jain et al., 2016 ) , which Corollary 2.2 (c) shows training weights do implicitly.

sections.heading: Calibration versus ranking.
sections.text: Post-hoc calibration ( Platt, 1999 ; Zadrozny and Elkan, 2002 ; Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana, 2005 ; Kull et al., 2017 ; Guo et al., 2017 ) optimizes a probability metric, and its effect on a ranking depends on whether the map is shared or class-wise: shared class-wise binning recovers the top-5 accuracy that independent per-class maps lose on ImageNet ( Patel et al., 2021 ) , intra-order-preserving maps are rank-preserving by construction ( Rahimi et al., 2020 ) , and in extreme multi-label classification a shared monotone map keeps precision@ k k untouched while per-label calibration is deferred to future work ( Ullah et al., 2025 ) ; label-wise monotone reranking after calibration ( Tae and Lee, 2026 ) targets the residual reliability of fixed decisions, not the cross-label scale that a training weight distorts, and has no policy for a label without calibration positives. Per-class residual offsets are Bayes-optimal for reranking when the distortion is class-separable ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , the case our intercept-only rung tests, but that residual is defined on a base model’s shortlist and is not traced to a training weight, whereas slippage is the gap between an intended ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} and what the learner realized, bounded by the step budget and broken by saturation; recommender systems calibrate within rank groups ( Sato, 2024 ) ; automated calibrator selection ( Abdelrahman et al., 2025 ) chooses by a probability metric rather than by the deployed ranking metric.

sections.heading: Next-basket recommendation.
sections.text: Next-basket recommendation scores every item from the ordered history of prior baskets and cuts the list at a fixed K K ( Yu et al., 2016 ) ; its benchmark canon ( Li et al., 2023 ) and the models it compares ( Hu et al., 2020 ; Ariannezhad et al., 2022 ) use the Instacart 2017 data ( Instacart, 2017 ) in this form, with the last basket held out and frequency rankers as the reference. Our Instacart experiments follow that formulation but ask what per-label weights do to a fixed one-vs-rest learner, not which model predicts the next basket best; the popularity row of Table 1 is that literature’s frequency baseline.

sections.heading: Recipe.
sections.text: Five steps, in order, for a one-vs-rest ranker over many rare labels. (1) Estimate marginals with an unweighted proper loss. If imbalance makes optimization hard, prefer a weight common to all labels, which is rank-neutral by Corollary 2.2 (a). (2) If label-specific weights are kept, cap the leaf step. A cap removes the saturation ties, which nothing post hoc can repair, at the price of leaving the intended shift unrealized: the inversion is then wrong in the other direction and calibration is what fixes the ranking ( Figure 3 ). A small cap compresses the scores until no per-label map recovers the cross-label order ( c = 0.3 c=0.3 above), which is why step 5 chooses the calibrator rather than fixing it. (3) Calibrate on a held-out split from the training period , never from the evaluation period. (4) Send labels without calibration positives to their prior, not through the identity. This choice, not the threshold or the split, decides whether the repair helps or hurts; where positives are merely scarce no τ \tau makes a per-label map safe (birds, medical). (5) Choose τ \tau , per-label versus shared, and whether to calibrate at all, by cross-validation inside the calibration split (Supplement Table S6): the objective is the deployed metric and the rule never touches test labels. Where that split does not predict the test data, no calibration is the safe default for an unweighted model; the shared map is not (more than 0.01 0.01 below raw in 9 of 110 cells). Where the pipeline allows it, keep the raw margin rather than the stored probability: it preserves the order inside the saturated cells, though not the cross-label scale. Without labels, the share of cells at exactly 1.0 1.0 and the number of distinct scores per label flag saturation and predict that the inversion will fail.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: • Scope of the large-scale evidence. Two recommendation benchmarks with 24 and 4,000 labels, two learner families and one headline weight regime ( w j = n − / n + w_{j}=n_{-}/n_{+} up to 8,248,932); the r \sqrt{r} and 10 ​ r 10r arms and the capped unweighted twins exist on Santander only, and MAP ​ @ ​ K \mathrm{MAP}@K is the only metric reported (recall and NDCG at K K , the next-basket canon, are not). MULAN replicates the collapse but not its scale (largest r = 3149 r=3149 ; Corel5k and delicious have 500 and 3,185 test rows) and does not locate the boundary; the two largest MULAN datasets were not run. • Only the step budget is tight. Without a cap we bound nothing; the realized shift is measurable only where no cell saturates, and the two estimators of the shift disagree on how much of it is realized ( 0.78 0.78 against 0.98 0.98 of ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} on Santander, 0.50 0.50 against 0.88 0.88 on Instacart) because they read different label sets. The two conditions of Figure 3 are an empirical association, not a proven characterization. • Single runs and a fixed configuration. Each matched pair is a single run. Retraining the Santander pair on a second machine with the same data, script, configuration and LightGBM version did not reproduce it bit for bit: the weighted model scored 0.111 0.111 raw against 0.117 0.117 , the unweighted one 0.808 0.808 against 0.808 0.808 (Supplement S7). Together with the 3 draws ( 0.092 ± 0.052 0.092\pm 0.052 ) this says that the depth of the weighted Santander collapse is run-dependent while every other rung is stable; the canonical arrays are archived with the release. The MLP pairs are single stochastic runs at one width and one epoch budget, evaluated under the test-split protocol only; the LightGBM configuration was fixed on Santander and not tuned for Instacart. • What the ceiling is, and where the selection rule fails. The oracle ceiling is the best per-label isotonic fit in squared loss read off at MAP ​ @ ​ K \mathrm{MAP}@K , not a bound on all post-hoc procedures; row-dependent calibrators ( Rahimi et al., 2020 ) are outside the separable class. No threshold in calibration positives separates harmful from harmless per-label calibration, and the cross-validated choice ends more than 0.01 0.01 below raw in 6 of 110 cells, where the calibration split does not predict the test file. Its grid ends at τ = 10 \tau=10 , which the rule picks in 23 of its 45 per-label choices; a wider grid was not run. The prior fallback is a floor for stationary catalogues: a label with test positives but no calibration positives is sent to the bottom of every row and the rule cannot see the loss; on Santander all 3 dead labels are also dead in the test split.

sections.heading: Conclusion.
sections.text: Per-label class weights change the target of one-vs-rest training from the marginal to a weighted odds, and on two recommendation benchmarks the textbook odds shift is the minor part of the resulting top- K K loss for the boosted pairs (23% on Santander, 32% on Instacart); the major part is odds-shift slippage, a realized shift that differs from ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} plus ties from saturation, which the analytic inversion cannot undo. What varies across learners and datasets is how much of the label set saturates, so the repair is what carries across learners and the inversion is not. Per-label calibration with a prior fallback supplies it up to the residue the ties impose, and the fallback, not the calibrator, decides its sign. Where the weight is not needed for optimization, a label-specific weight bought nothing for the ranking on our benchmarks; where it is, it should be followed by per-label calibration before the top- K K decision.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: All scores, calibrators, tables and figures are produced by the released experiment and publication sources ( https://github.com/souldrive7/odds-shift-slippage ) from fixed prediction arrays (SHA-256 recorded in the result files; regenerated from the public Kaggle data by the released training scripts) and the public MULAN ARFF files (content hashes recorded). Every run’s configuration and seed are recorded, the dead-label policy is a named argument of every calibrator, and the supplement is an ancillary file of this preprint.

One-vs-rest rankers that show each user the top- K K of many rare labels usually counter imbalance with a per-label positive-class weight, scale_pos_weight = n − / n + =n_{-}/n_{+} . Elkan’s identity says such a weight shifts label j j ’s log-odds by ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} , so the model ranks by weighted odds rather than by the marginal that is Bayes-optimal for precision@ K K , and it suggests inverting the shift afterwards; what a finite learner does with a weight in the thousands, and which repair then works, has not been measured. We call the gap between the promised shift and the realized one odds-shift slippage and measure it on matched pairs of LightGBM and MLP models that differ only in the weights. On Santander the weight takes MAP ​ @ ​ 7 \mathrm{MAP}@7 from 0.808 0.808 to 0.117 0.117 ; for the boosted pairs the ideal odds shift accounts for 23% of that loss (32% on Instacart; 98% for an MLP pair on the same rows) and slippage for the rest. We prove that a booster whose leaf steps are capped at c c realizes at most T ​ η ​ c T\eta c nat of shift in T T rounds at rate η \eta , which a cap sweep confirms, and show that without a cap saturated cells tie at exactly 1.0 1.0 , beyond the reach of any separable map. The analytic inversion therefore pays only where the shift was realized and nothing saturated, whereas per-label isotonic regression returns the Santander model to 0.784 0.784 ( 0.780 0.780 with the calibrator fitted on the validation period) — but only if labels without calibration positives are mapped to their prior rather than passed through. On 11 public MULAN benchmarks and 5 learners the weighted model loses more than half of its MAP ​ @ ​ K \mathrm{MAP}@K in 8 of 55 cells, and on delicious and Corel5k the same repair returns it to the unweighted level; per-label calibration hurts where positives are scarce, a harm that a cross-validated rule removes for the default learner. The recipe — estimate marginals unweighted, calibrate per label with an explicit prior fallback, choose the calibrator on the calibration split, then decide at top- K K — is released as oddslip . 1. Introduction Ranking many binary labels within a row is the operational core of product recommendation, tagging and risk triage: for each customer the system scores every product, sorts, and shows the top K K ( Jain et al., 2016 ; Menon et al., 2019 ) . The labels are almost always imbalanced, and the most common remedy in gradient-boosting practice is a per-label positive-class weight, scale_pos_weight in XGBoost and LightGBM ( Chen and Guestrin, 2016 ; Ke et al., 2017 ) , for which the XGBoost documentation suggests n − / n + n_{-}/n_{+} ( XGBoost developers, 2026 ) ; neural multi-label models use the same recipe as pos_weight . Label-specific weights are not a free choice when the deliverable is a per-row ranking. Ranking labels by their marginal p i ​ j = Pr ⁡ ( y i ​ j = 1 ∣ x i ) p_{ij}=\Pr(y_{ij}=1\mid x_{i}) is Bayes-optimal for precision@ K K , and one-vs-rest training with a proper loss is consistent for it ( Menon et al., 2019 ; Wydmuch et al., 2018 ) . A positive-class weight w w moves the population minimizer of a proper loss from p p to w ​ p / ( w ​ p + 1 − p ) wp/(wp+1-p) , an odds shift by w w ( Elkan, 2001 ; Saerens et al., 2002 ) . Together the two facts say that a label-specific w j w_{j} makes the model rank by w j ⋅ odds ⁡ ( p i ​ j ) w_{j}\cdot\mathrm{odds}(p_{ij}) , a different ranking whenever the weights differ. What the classical account leaves open is what a finite learner does when w j w_{j} is in the thousands, as the recommended value is for rare labels, and which post-hoc repair then works. Independent per-class calibration maps are known to lose top- k k accuracy in multi-class settings ( Patel et al., 2021 ) , and the extreme multi-label literature deliberately uses one shared monotone map, deferring per-label calibration to future work ( Ullah et al., 2025 ) . Neither measures the cross-label consequence of training weights on a top- K K benchmark, nor what a calibrator does with labels that have no calibration positives. Figure 2 gives our answer on two product-recommendation benchmarks, Santander and Instacart, each on a pair of LightGBM models that differ only in the weights. Applying the ideal odds shift to the unweighted model reproduces only a minority of the loss the trained weighted model actually suffers. We call the remainder odds-shift slippage : the shift the learner realizes is not the shift the weight asked for. Figure 1 sketches the two regimes that produce it. A leaf-step cap keeps the realized shift below ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} ( Proposition 2.4 ); without a cap the learner realizes the shift on the labels where it is still defined, while elsewhere cells saturate into ties that no per-label map can reorder ( Lemma 2.3 ). Among the configurations we evaluated, analytic inversion improves only those that combine a near-intended realized shift with no observed saturation ( Figure 3 ); per-label calibration repairs the ordered part, provided that a label without calibration positives is mapped to its prior rather than passed through ( Remark 2 ). Contributions (1) Odds-shift slippage, decomposed. Using Elkan’s identity as a what-if device, we split the top- K K loss of a weighted one-vs-rest ranker into the ideal odds shift and the loss beyond it, the slippage, which itself splits into the component that a per-label monotone map fitted on calibration data recovers and a residue above the in-sample per-label ceiling ( Figure 2 A, Table 1 ). For the boosted pairs the shift accounts for 23% of the observed loss on Santander ( 20.3 ± 2.3 % 20.3\pm 2.3\% over three train-row draws) and 32% on Instacart; the share is a property of the pair, since an MLP pair on the same Santander rows gives up 98% of its loss to the same ideal shift. Logit adjustment and residual reranking ( Menon et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) correct a trained score; neither measures how far a training weight’s intended shift was realized, which is what the decomposition isolates. (2) A step budget that makes the account falsifiable. Proposition 2.4 bounds the realized per-label shift of a booster with leaf-step cap c c by T ​ η ​ c T\eta c whatever the weight, and Corollary 2.5 says when the analytic inversion is exact. A sweep of 5 caps on both benchmarks keeps every realized maximum inside its budget with no saturation ( Figure 2 B); without a cap the shift is identifiable only on labels with no saturated cell, where its median is close to ln ⁡ w j \ln w_{j} . Among the evaluated models the inversion pays only for the two that realized most of the shift and saturated nothing ( Figure 3 ), an association rather than a proven condition; and an unweighted twin trained with the same cap matches the calibrated capped weighted arm, so on Santander, the one dataset with such twins, the cap, not the weight, is what helps; we know of no earlier statement of when the analytic inversion ( Elkan, 2001 ) can be exact for a booster under a leaf-step cap. (3) Per-label calibration with a prior fallback is the repair that travels, with its selection rule. Per-label isotonic regression with dead labels mapped to their prior returns the weighted Santander booster to within 0.003 0.003 of its in-sample ceiling under the test-split protocol and within 0.01 0.01 under the deployment protocol; a shared map repairs nothing beyond tie resolution ( Remark 1 ), and the identity fallback turns the same calibrator into a loss ( Remark 2 ). The collapse and its repair reproduce on 11 MULAN benchmarks and 5 learners ( Figure 4 ), where the calibrator also hurts an unweighted model with scarce calibration positives; a cross-validated choice inside the calibration split removes that harm for the default learner and fails in 6 of 110 cells.
